Market Cap: Compare valuation with verified supply and pool depth.
A large displayed valuation is supported by little executable liquidity.
Liquidity: Pool depth grows alongside activity and quoted exits remain practical.
Liquidity shrinks or a modest sale has a large quoted impact.
Liquidity vs Market Cap: Compare similarly valued tokens using pool depth and actual quotes.
Treat equal market caps as equal exit capacity.
Volume: Activity persists across time windows and is supported by varied participation.
A brief volume spike or repetitive churn is treated as durable demand.
Holders: Ownership appears to broaden after checking related addresses.
Holder count grows through dust transfers or wallets controlled by one actor.
Token Supply: Supply, reserved allocations, and permission changes can be accounted for.
New minting or unclear allocations can add unexpected sellable supply.
Price Impact: The intended order is checked against a current executable quote.
Order size is large relative to pool depth, even if small relative to market cap.
Bonding Curve: Curve progress and early ownership are checked together.
Progress accelerates while cheap inventory stays concentrated.
Graduation: The destination pool and seeded liquidity are verified.
A migration label is mistaken for proof of liquidity or continuation.
DEX: The exact contract, pool, route, and fees match the intended trade.
A matching ticker leads to the wrong contract or a thin secondary pool.
Snipers: Early inventory, prior sales, and remaining balances are traced.
Cheap early inventory is large relative to the pool's exit capacity.
Fresh Wallets: Funding and trade history are checked before inferring independence.
Many newly funded addresses repeat the same entry and transfer pattern.
Slippage: Tolerance and quoted impact are reviewed separately before submission.
Tolerance is increased repeatedly just to make an unexplained failure execute.
Spread: Compare executable buy and sell quotes including fees.
The chart price hides a costly immediate round trip.
MEV / Sandwiching: Review execution protection, quotes, and the actual transaction result.
A large order with broad tolerance gives adverse execution more room.
Top Holders: Separate pool, burn, exchange, and ordinary owner addresses.
Sellable supply is concentrated across a few related wallets.
Dev / Creator Wallet: Creator allocations and subsequent transfers are accounted for.
The visible creator balance falls while related wallets receive inventory.
Insiders: Multiple independent pieces of evidence support a suspected relationship.
Connected early wallets sell together around promotional events.
Bundles: Distinguish transaction bundling from inferred common wallet ownership.
A suspected cluster controls substantial cheap inventory and begins selling.
Bundle Push: Activity continues after the original coordinated buyers stop buying.
The same wallets support the rise and distribute into new arrivals.
Wallet Clusters: Funding, transfers, timing, and behavior support a qualified hypothesis.
One shared exchange withdrawal or similar trade is treated as identity proof.
Wallet Funding: Trace multiple hops and distinguish shared services from shared control.
Repeated fund splitting and linked transfers obscure one actor's inventory.
Smart Money / KOL Wallets: Wallet attribution, complete history, and remaining exposure are checked.
A reputation label substitutes for evidence or encourages copying a late entry.
Cost Basis: Separate observed purchases from transfers and missing history.
A current holding value is mistaken for how much the wallet paid.
Realized vs Unrealized P&L: Recorded buys, sells, fees, and remaining inventory reconcile.
A remaining balance conceals that most capital has already been recovered.
Accumulation: Repeated purchases and balance increases support the interpretation.
Transfers or one support buyer create the appearance of broad accumulation.
Distribution: Inventory reductions are traced and buyers continue absorbing sales.
Related wallets steadily unload while price and promotional activity stay strong.
Supply Absorption: Repeated selling meets continuing buying from varied participants.
One wallet supports price and disappears when selling intensifies.
Organic Buying: Evidence suggests varied participants and activity persists without one cluster.
Many buy transactions come from the same coordinated source.
Paper Hands: Describe observed holding time and sales without guessing motivation.
Repeated short-term exits exceed incoming demand.
Conviction Holders: Balances and holding history are examined alongside past sales.
A stable balance is assumed to prove conviction despite transfers or prior profit-taking.
Support / Base: Several retests meet buying within the observed period.
A single bounce is drawn as support despite repeated lower lows.
Resistance / Ceiling: Repeated tests and surrounding flow are compared over time.
Large selling repeatedly rejects the area while buyers weaken.
Breakout: The move holds above the prior area and survives a retest.
A brief wick or one large buy supplies the entire breakout thesis.
Fake Breakout: Reassess when price loses the old ceiling; wait for new evidence.
Price falls back into the old range as selling increases.
Repricing: A new valuation range persists with continuing activity and liquidity.
A short pump is labelled a new base before the market accepts it.
Pullback: The decline meets buying near a repeatedly observed support area.
Support fails while liquidity and buying activity deteriorate.
Panic Dump: Reassess available liquidity and subsequent flow before drawing conclusions.
Selling overwhelms depth and executable quotes deteriorate rapidly.
Entry Liquidity: The planned order fits the current quote and pool depth.
Entering in one order materially raises your own average price.
Exit Liquidity: Review current exit quotes, depth, and ongoing demand.
Paper profit assumes future buyers will absorb a large position.
Narrative: The story is supported by sources linked to the exact token.
A familiar name or compelling story is treated as proof of identity or demand.
Catalyst: A primary source confirms what changes and when.
Rumours or an announced date are treated as guaranteed new buying.
Social Momentum: Discussion broadens across independent participants and persists over time.
Repeated posts from a small group inflate the apparent audience.
CT / KOL Shilling: Separate promotional claims from source evidence and disclosed incentives.
Coordinated promotion coincides with early holders reducing inventory.
Attention Rotation: Compare attention evidence with sampled activity across themes and chains.
A token is assessed in isolation as participation moves elsewhere.
Chain Narrative: Chain-level claims are checked against sources and token-specific activity.
A popular chain is treated as sufficient evidence for every token on it.
Meme Lifecycle: The strategy matches observed launch stage, attention, and ownership changes.
An early-launch playbook is applied to a mature distribution phase.
Liquidity Lock / Burn: Verify the specific pool, position controller, lock terms, and expiry.
A lock badge is assumed to cover every pool and every risk.
Rug Pull: Investigate permissions, liquidity control, and supply movements together.
A controller can extract liquidity or sell hidden inventory into buyers.
Honeypot: Independent selling and current restrictions are checked through external evidence.
Buying succeeds while ordinary wallets cannot exit on comparable terms.
Mint Authority: Verify current authority and supply history for the exact mint.
An operator can create unexpected inventory and sell it into the pool.
Freeze Authority: Check authority status and relevant token permissions onchain.
A controller can restrict accounts while buyers assume unrestricted transfers.
Wash Trading: Compare transaction patterns with ownership and participation evidence.
Circular funding and repetitive trades manufacture apparent demand.
Market Maker / Bot Activity: Distinguish automated liquidity provision from new buying demand.
Most displayed activity disappears when one bot or operator stops.
Hidden Distribution: Trace transfers and total related-wallet balances through time.
Fresh addresses receive inventory and sell while top-holder concentration appears to improve.
Unlocked-Liquidity Warning: Verify who controls each position and whether withdrawal is possible.
A controller can remove the depth on which an exit depends.
Position Size: Planned exposure reflects acceptable loss and executable exit capacity.
Size grows from excitement while liquidity remains thin.
Stop Loss: An exit condition is paired with realistic execution assumptions.
A trigger price is treated as a guaranteed fill or loss cap.
Scaling In: Every addition has stated evidence and a maximum total exposure.
Repeated averaging down quietly exceeds the original risk plan.
Scaling Out: Planned reductions consider executable quotes and remaining exposure.
Targets exist on paper but position size overwhelms available buyers.
Taking Initial Capital Out: Recovered proceeds are tracked after costs and remaining exposure is reviewed.
The remaining position is called risk-free and ignored.
Risk / Reward: Compare plausible outcomes with invalidation, costs, and execution constraints.
An extreme theoretical target hides immediate downside or a difficult exit.
Survivorship Bias: Review losers and failed launches alongside visible winners.
Only exceptional winners are used to judge how easy the strategy is.
Exit Strategy: Reasons to reduce or leave are written before entry and reviewed as evidence changes.
An entry plan is detailed but the exit depends on emotion or new hype.
Entry Liquidity vs Exit Liquidity: Entry quotes and possible exit conditions are assessed separately.
Easy buying during hype is assumed to imply easy selling later.
The Core Meme-Trading Question: Connect ownership, cost, current behavior, and demand using traceable evidence.
A compelling chart replaces unanswered questions about supply and exit capacity.
Market Maturity: The venue and current trading conditions are verified.
A listing is mistaken for guaranteed liquidity or lower risk.
